title: The grove and the cave
hookLine: an old grove, a deep cave, a river's source: places that stir a sense of the sacred (Letters 41)

lines: THE HAIR ON YOUR ARMS LIFTS.
cards: Under very old trees, voices drop. Often nobody has to ask. The light goes green and dim, the noise of the road falls away, and even someone who'd never call themselves religious may feel the hair on their arms lift.
The same letter to Lucilius goes on to describe exactly this feeling, in three kinds of places. And then Seneca turns the whole thing around.

teach.h: THE GROVE THAT SHUTS OUT THE SKY.
teach.b: Come upon a grove of old trees grown taller than usual, he writes, their branches woven so thick they shut out the sky, and the height of the forest, the hush of the place and your wonder at that deep, unbroken shade will make you believe in a divine presence.
A mountain hollowed into a deep cave, by nature, not by hands, will strike your soul with a sense of something holy.
The Romans honored the sources of great rivers; they set altars where a sudden stream bursts from hiding, and some pools were thought sacred for their darkness or their depth. Then the turn.

teach.h: THE SAME AWE, IN A PERSON.
teach.b: If you see someone unafraid in danger, untouched by cravings, happy in hard times, calm in a storm, he asks, won't the same awe come over you?
Won't you say that something too great for that small body has come down into it?
Seneca doesn't dismiss the grove and the cave. His point is that the same holiness can shine through a steady human being.
The old forest teaches you what awe feels like, so you can recognize it again, in a hospital waiting room, in a person holding steady.

how: Some people on their own path keep a favorite old tree, spring or quiet place they return to, and some, following Seneca, also pay attention to the steady people who stir the same awe.

games.q: you've just felt awe in an ancient forest. where does Seneca say you might feel it again?
o: in a person who is calm and unafraid in hard times.
nowhere: it was a trick of the light.
games.why: Seneca turns from grove, cave and spring to the person whose steadiness seems too great for one small body.

practice: Stand near the oldest tree you know, or picture one clearly: the bark, the height, the light through the leaves, and let your breathing slow to its pace.
Then bring to mind one person who carries that same steadiness, and hold the two together.

wordCard.voice: Lucus. Seneca's word for a sacred grove, where the hush and the deep shade can make you believe in a divine presence. Today's word.
